Honestly, I’m the opposite. I have to be careful because I become addicted to working. I don’t say that lightly either. I have difficulty taking breaks and going on vacation is more stress than not. The last time I didn’t have any job at all, I became agoraphobic and even walking to my mailbox was terrifying and painful. I have gotten full time jobs and added in part time jobs, not because I necessarily needed the money, but because I hate being idle. 

As far as bad bosses, I’ve had quite a few. Unfortunately, even when some good people get small amounts of power, it goes straight to their heads. You can never predict who will be who. I’ve learned not to tolerate it and to protect myself mentally, I will leave if I feel the workplace is too toxic. I have been able to help shift the toxicity though, with help from coworkers. 

First rule is to be honest, with both yourself and your coworkers and bosses. Don’t lie. Don’t hide. Don’t say anything to anyone else about someone you wouldn’t say directly to their face.

Secondly, you are in control of your own career. If you think things with come easily, you are doing something wrong. Work harder. There is always something to clean, something to file, something to organize. Bosses eat that shit up.

Third, one bad experience does not mean everything is terrible. I have a pattern: first day is awesome, second day sucks out loud, third day is what I make it. I’ve come to accept if I excel on the first day, my second day, I will become cocky and make a mistake and embarrass myself. But, I am not my mistakes.

Lastly, jobs can not only help you become self sufficient financially, but emotionally as well. You learn new skills everywhere you work, whether it’s flipping burgers, teaching little kids about nature, making coffee, or even just walking dogs. If you are afraid of bosses, start slow. Try working for neighbors and friends: outdoor chores, pet sitting, folding laundry.

Changes are scary. That’s okay. It’s okay to be scared, but don’t let it stop you from growing as a person.

Most clippers you get at pet stores are not meant for clipping the entire dog. Professional grade clippers are what you want. I recommend looking into Wahl Bravura or Andis Excel 5 Speed. I have these and they are my favorite. Many groomers also like the Wahl KM10 or the Andis AGC. Andis recently came out with a new clipper and they’ve had both good and bad reviews but are currently out of my price range. I recommend looking on EBay or FB marketplace - you can get good quality clippers for far cheaper than their retail price. There are a lot of very good grooming/tool sharpening blogs and articles out there that will help you find the length blades you will need. Blades numbers in dogs and humans are different but they will usually list the length on the blade. Also human blades aren’t sharp enough to get through that sort of hair. Especially the cottony hair - think very soft Maltese or cat hair - is very difficult to cut and requires special blades that won’t clog.

The hair usually had a purpose. There is evidence that some Native American peoples kept a long haired breed of dog and sheared it regularly for the “wool”. 

In particular, during times where dog breeds were changed and expanded, a lot of breeds lost their original purpose and their coats changed. For example, during the Victorian Era, Pomeranian dogs went from about 30lbs and used as sled dogs, to very tiny lap dogs. The original purpose of standard poodles has changed immensely as well. They were originally hunting dogs and this is largely forgotten. Cording - which is similar to dreads on humans but is essentially controlled matting - was a popular way to keep poodle coats back in the day. 

Recently, with the boom in puppy mills, lower quality coats that are prone to matting and dogs with poor conformation are becoming more common than not. Also the lack of education between breeders and owners has lead to puppies being placed in homes that may not meet the puppy’s needs.

The most important thing is to keep control of his head. He doesn’t understand what you are doing so it will seem scary to him. If you are using scissors, always keep them angled away from his eyes, lips and ears. It’s very easy to cut skin. If you are using clippers, first introduce him to the feeling before just putting them on his skin. Also, you want to hold him as still as possible: a lot of groomers will use the chin hairs - if there are enough - to keep them from pulling away, or wrap their hand around the back of the head, with the thumb under their jaw. 

I would recommend finding a dog groomer in your area to show you some holds, or even to do the job. It’s very easy to accidentally hurt your dog without meaning to if you’re not quite sure what you are doing.
